headline: CMG tightening grip on domestic iron ore procurement through centralised platform, creating structural pricing risk for Australian miners
reasoning: China's CMG is pushing domestic mills to procure iron ore through a centralised platform, restricting who they can buy from, how much, and when. This follows CMG reportedly pressuring mills not to buy certain Rio Tinto spot cargoes. Widnell sees this as a continuation of a pattern where miners concede on pricing terms and CMG returns for more. The key long-term concern is that increased CMG control could lead to artificial suppression of iron ore prices. Widnell describes this as the 'new normal' for many years until China feels it has more control over iron ore price volatility.

Um, you know, sort of pushing some of the, the mills, um, not to buy, um, supposedly not to buy cargoes, um, from Rio Tinto. Um, in terms of some spot tons, um, some, some specific brands. So it's while it's constricting sort of liquidity on the, on the physical market on the front end, it's obviously, you know, we can all see what's glaringly obvious on the, on the back end of the curve and that, you know, basically, you know, CMG trying to exert more control over pricing.

headline: Chinese hot metal production bottomed on 2 July and is now ramping gradually, supporting iron ore prices into Golden September
reasoning: Thermal satellite heat map data from blast furnaces, coke ovens, and basic oxygen furnaces across Chinese steel mills shows hot metal production — a proxy for steel output — troughed on 2 July and has since been rising consistently. Mills are ramping up capacity utilisation to meet demand through the 'Golden September' and October peak construction season before year-end subsides. Weather disruptions (torrential rains in the north, heat waves in the south) had suppressed demand but are now easing. Widnell expects iron ore to gradually climb through year-end, recovering from the year's low of around $92.85 to current levels near $96.65.
quote: So what that data is currently telling us now, that sort of hot metal production, which is the proxy for steel production in China, um, actually bottomed out on the 2nd of July. And now we can see sort of quite a consistent and gradual ramp up in activity. Um, and so we're seeing those heat signatures get bigger and bigger and bigger and more, um, more high frequency as well. And so that's telling us that they're ramping up to meet that. Those last two bastions of, um, higher sort of steel demand, um, through the back end of the year, which falls, as you said, in September and October before sort of the market sort of then subsides, um, through the end of the year. And so they're obviously ramping up production now to feed that higher demand, um, as it comes back after, you know, um, torrential rains in the north and, um, excessive heat waves in the south. So I think we're also seeing that on the on the steel price as well. There's there's better demand out there. And also that's keeping iron ore also relatively well bid as well. So that's why, you know, we've recovered from I think it was one two weeks ago where we're trading at sort of the year's lows of 9285. And that's why we're sort of $4 up. So we're sort of expecting iron ore to sort of keep gradually, um, sort of climbing through the end of the year.

headline: Navigate Commodities flags China's likely orchestration of Radiant World's downfall as a strategic move to consolidate iron ore trading through CMG and tighten Beijing's grip on physical supply
reasoning: Widnell highlights that Singapore-based physical iron ore trader Radiant World, which traded around 60–70 million tonnes of physical iron ore, is under intense scrutiny, with banks and commodity trading counterparties pulling financing. He notes China has been making noise about Radiant for years and finds the timing suspicious, suggesting this is not merely about accounting irregularities. His thesis is that if Radiant exits the market, China's state-controlled CMG (China Minmetals Group) would be the primary beneficiary, as miners previously selling to Radiant would be pushed to do spot tonnes directly through CMG or its domestic platform, or onto long-term contracts. This effectively concentrates physical iron ore trade in state hands and reduces secondary market liquidity, serving China's strategic interests.
quote: I think the timing aspect is quite, quite interesting. Um, obviously, if um, sadly, it looks like sort of, uh, radiant, um, is uh, is the subject of a lot of attention at the moment and now sort of banks and what other sort of commodity traders that finance them are all backing away from them? And that's that sort of paints. It's an interesting picture in itself that, you know, they might have some, um, their own liquidity problems in terms of financing sort of iron ore, uh, trade on the secondary market. Um, obviously, if that does happen, that means a player that was trading sort of 60, 70 million tonnes worth of physical iron ore, um, might eventually sort of exit the market. So again, it then sort of constricts that secondary physical trade and, and guess who the beneficiary is. Um, you know, um CMG then push the miners that were selling to radiant to do more spot tons directly through CMG Morton through their own domestic platform, more tonnes on long term um contracts.

headline: Navigate Commodities bullish on iron ore, sees price climbing to $100–$105/t by year-end on hot metal production and seasonal restocking demand
reasoning: Atilla Widnell notes iron ore has recovered from year lows of $92.85 and expects a gradual climb through year-end. He points to blast furnace production ramp-ups and satellite-confirmed hot metal production increases in China as key demand drivers. Seasonally, Q4 iron ore futures almost always trade higher than Q3 because Chinese steel mills maintain elevated operating rates to restock ahead of Chinese New Year. Thermal satellite imagery corroborates this pattern, showing higher Q4 demand versus Q3. He targets $100–$105 per wet metric tonne by year-end, which he acknowledges is relatively optimistic versus most market consensus.
quote: I'm still relatively bullish, I think, like, um, we might find some resistance at 100. I still think we could do probably 100, 105 bucks by the end of the year. Um, that's quite optimistic, but, um, yeah, never say never. Hot metal production in China and therefore iron ore consumption should keep on climbing through the end of the year, because once we get through sort of gold and September and silver October, sort of hot metal production, steel production sort of plateaus a little bit, but it still remains relatively elevated because what they're doing is they keep their maintaining higher operating rates, um, to restock in December and January ahead of Chinese New Year.

headline: CMG negotiations could create short-term upside pricing shock but are a longer-term negative
reasoning: Atilla Widnell flags that CMG negotiations with FMG (Fortescue) have the ability to create a short-term upside pricing shock for iron ore. However, over the longer term, as CMG takes more control over long-term contracts and pricing power, this is a negative development for iron ore producers including FMG. The structural shift in pricing power towards CMG is seen as an unfavourable dynamic for the sector.
quote: CMG um, negotiations with FMG have the ability to sort of create that upside sort of pricing shock. Um, but longer term it is a negative. Um, as CMG takes more control over long term um, contracts and over pricing power over iron ore, unfortunately.
episode_title: Strike while the iron's hot...or not?

headline: BHP Port Hedland strike is a temporary non-event for iron ore supply, with rally likely to be sold into
reasoning: Widnell notes that BHP workers voted for an eight-hour strike on July 16, which pushed iron ore futures back toward $99/tonne. However, he views the supply disruption as fleeting and largely inconsequential — BHP can quickly make up any lost tonnage. Chinese steel mills are sitting on 160-170 million tonnes of stockpiles, making any short-term Australian supply disruption essentially background noise. He expects the rally to be sold into within days.
quote: I mean, obviously the markets sort of rallied on the back of that. Um, but it's it's really quite temporary. I mean, it's only going to be an eight hour strike. Um, but that's obviously been sufficient, um, to push iron ore back up towards, uh, 99 bucks a tonne. Um, but, you know, as we see it, it's sort of a quickly favorable rally that most likely will be sold into in the coming days. So yeah, we're looking very closely at that BHP strike. As you say, it's only eight hours.
episode_title: Strike while the iron's hot...or not?

headline: Weak Chinese hot metal output is the dominant near-term iron ore price driver, with seasonal trough expected through July-August
reasoning: Navigate Commodities monitors 228 blast furnaces across China daily via thermal satellite imagery and is seeing a contraction in hot metal output — the key proxy for iron ore demand. Steel margins in China are running at -100 to -200 RMB per tonne, meaning most mills are loss-making and cutting production harder than seasonal norms. Monsoonal rains in the north and heat waves in the south are suppressing construction activity and associated steel demand. Widnell expects the production trough to persist into August before a seasonal uptick in Q4 as weather improves and restocking begins.
quote: we're monitoring 228 blast furnaces across China every single day using thermal, um, satellite imagery. So we can see that there's a contraction in hot metal output across China, which is the proxy for iron ore demand in China. Um, and so every year without fail, um, sort of Chinese, um, sort of activity sort of subsides into July, um, sometimes in August, depending where sort of steel margins are currently sitting. And right now that is probably one of the biggest drivers that still, margins in China are trading at a -100 to 200 R&B a ton, which is quite pertinent. So what that means is that they're obviously all majority are loss making at the moment. And so they're having to pull back probably harder than they would typically for this time of year.
episode_title: Strike while the iron's hot...or not?
